With this network context in place, the following section introduces the significant proteins identified in the enrichment analysis and considers their possible relevance in a more detailed and sequential manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the proteins listed, TREM2 is the most directly relevant to depression because it is centrally involved in microglial biology, neuroinflammation, and neuron-glia interactions. Depression is increasingly understood to involve immune dysregulation and inflammatory signaling within the central nervous system, and microglia are key mediators of these processes. The reported requirement of TREM2-TYROBP signaling for phagocytosis of apoptotic neurons and for control of microglial superoxide production indicates a role in synaptic and neuronal homeostasis, processes that are highly pertinent to stress-related neural remodeling and depressive symptomatology. Moreover, the observation that this pathway promotes pro-inflammatory microglial responses after nerve injury suggests a plausible mechanistic link to inflammation-associated depression, in which activated innate immune pathways contribute to neuronal dysfunction and behavioral changes. Its additional effects on IL10 production and dendritic-cell immunoregulation further support the view that TREM2 participates in balancing inflammatory versus anti-inflammatory responses, a theme strongly implicated in depression pathophysiology.[PubMed:15471863](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15471863) [PubMed:9647200](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647200) [PubMed:15728241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241) [PubMed:16715077](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16715077) [PubMed:21727189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21727189) [PubMed:17086186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) [PubMed:18957693](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18957693) [PubMed:18685038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [PubMed:25690660](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660) [PubMed:21257958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958) [PubMed:18691974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18691974) [PubMed:12569157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12569157) [PubMed:14969392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969392) 

Moving from a primarily microglia centered candidate to a broader regulator of tissue signaling, TGFB1 also appears noteworthy in this context. TGFB1 stands out because transforming growth factor-beta signaling is broadly involved in immune regulation, tissue remodeling, apoptosis, and neuroplasticity, all of which are relevant to depression. Although the specific function provided here concerns promotion of cell death during mammary gland involution, the underlying biology points to a potent role in apoptotic signaling and tissue homeostasis. In the context of depression, TGFB-family pathways are of interest because excessive or dysregulated apoptotic and inflammatory signaling can impair neuronal resilience, alter synaptic connectivity, and contribute to stress-induced brain changes. Thus, even though the annotation is not brain-specific, TGFB1 remains noteworthy as a signaling molecule with plausible relevance to depression through its broader roles in inflammatory control and cell survival-death balance.

A related but somewhat more systemic line of reasoning applies to FGF23, which may connect bone associated biology with aging and metabolic pathways relevant to brain function. FGF23 is potentially relevant to depression because the annotation connects it to Klotho biology and modulation of insulin/IGF1 signaling, pathways increasingly associated with aging, metabolic dysfunction, and brain health. Depression frequently co-occurs with accelerated biological aging and metabolic abnormalities, and insulin/IGF1 signaling has been implicated in neuroplasticity, stress responsiveness, and cognitive dysfunction. Klotho itself has attracted attention for neuroprotective and anti-aging properties, raising the possibility that dysregulation of this axis could influence vulnerability to depressive symptoms, particularly in aging or medically ill populations. Although the evidence in the provided annotation is indirect and not depression-specific, FGF23 is notable because it intersects with systemic pathways that can shape central nervous system resilience.

In a similar vein, PSAP appears relevant through molecular processes that influence transcriptional regulation and cellular survival. PSAP is of interest because it links epigenetic repression, messenger ribonucleic acid splicing, and apoptosis regulation, all of which are biologically plausible contributors to depression. The involvement of PSAP in SIN3-HDAC1-mediated transcriptional repression suggests a connection to chromatin remodeling, a mechanism widely implicated in stress responses and antidepressant action. Its role in the splicing modulation of BCL2L1/Bcl-X is particularly relevant, since altered balance between pro-survival and pro-apoptotic signaling may influence neuronal integrity and stress susceptibility. In depression, disrupted ribonucleic acid processing and maladaptive transcriptional programs have been reported in both neurons and glial cells; therefore, a factor that coordinates repression and apoptotic splice choice could contribute to disease mechanisms involving impaired cellular resilience. While the annotation does not provide direct psychiatric evidence, PSAP stands out as a mechanistically rich candidate with potential relevance to depression-related molecular pathology.

Finally, SCARB2 appears less directly connected to depression than TREM2, TGFB1, FGF23, or PSAP, but it may still be relevant within a broader neuroimmune framework. SCARB2 appears less directly connected to depression than TREM2, TGFB1, FGF23, or PSAP, but it may still be relevant in a broader neuroimmune context. Its role as a viral receptor suggests potential involvement in host-pathogen interactions and infection-triggered inflammatory responses. Since infectious and post-infectious immune activation can precipitate neuroinflammation and depressive symptoms in some individuals, proteins that mediate microbial entry or host response may have indirect importance. However, based on the functional information provided here, SCARB2 has a comparatively limited and less specific connection to depression mechanisms.

### carbohydrate binding (GO:0030246) 

Carbohydrate binding is a molecular function in which a protein selectively and non-covalently recognizes carbohydrate structures, including simple sugars, complex oligosaccharides, polysaccharides, and chemically modified sugar derivatives. This function is biologically important because carbohydrates are major components of the cell surface and extracellular environment, where they regulate cell adhesion, receptor activation, immune recognition, trafficking, and intercellular communication. Proteins with carbohydrate-binding capacity include lectins, lipopolysaccharide-binding proteins, glycan-recognizing receptors, extracellular matrix-associated proteins, and signaling regulators that respond to glycolipids or glycoproteins. In the nervous system, carbohydrate-dependent interactions influence synapse formation, neuronal morphology, glial activation, blood-brain and gut-barrier signaling, and inflammatory communication between peripheral tissues and the brain. Because depression is increasingly understood as a disorder involving not only neurotransmitter imbalance but also neuroinflammation, stress-axis dysregulation, synaptic dysfunction, and altered gut-brain communication, carbohydrate-binding proteins and carbohydrate-responsive signaling systems are plausible mechanistic contributors. The pathway is therefore best viewed not as a single linear cascade, but as a functional category that links sugar-containing ligands or glycoconjugates to immune, metabolic, and neural processes relevant to depressive pathophysiology. 

Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that carbohydrate binding may be related to depression through three convergent themes: immune-inflammatory signaling, gut-liver-brain communication, and more direct carbohydrate-derived regulation of neural function. A large plasma proteomics study found that proteins associated with depression were significantly enriched in carbohydrate binding together with phosphoinositide three-kinase and protein kinase B signaling, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells signaling, and cytokine-receptor interaction pathways, indicating that carbohydrate-binding proteins are embedded within the inflammatory molecular architecture of depression rather than acting only as isolated markers (PubMed:41500316). This interpretation is further supported by studies centered on lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, a protein that recognizes a carbohydrate-rich bacterial cell wall component and may link intestinal barrier disturbance to systemic inflammation. In individuals undergoing carbohydrate malabsorption testing, interleukin six was positively associated with depressive symptoms and with altered tryptophan-to-kynurenine metabolism, while lipopolysaccharide-binding protein correlated with the kynurenine-to-tryptophan ratio, supporting a model in which carbohydrate-related gut dysfunction may promote inflammatory and metabolic changes relevant to depression (PubMed:33312105). Although one cross-sectional study in obstructive sleep apnea did not detect a direct association between lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and depressive symptom severity, it still linked lipopolysaccharide-binding protein to systemic inflammatory status, suggesting context dependence rather than absence of biological relevance (PubMed:40101844). A recent review of intestinal permeability biomarkers further supports the possibility that carbohydrate-recognizing innate immune mediators may help define an inflammation-related subtype of depression, even if clinical standardization remains incomplete (PubMed:41155365). Mechanistic support also comes from an animal study showing that *Bupleurum chinense* reduced hepatic lipopolysaccharide-binding protein expression, suppressed nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells signaling, restored monoamine biosynthesis, and improved depression-like behavior, thereby connecting a carbohydrate-binding inflammatory mediator to depressive phenotypes through the liver-brain axis (PubMed:41794258). Beyond peripheral inflammation, carbohydrate-derived molecules may also act more directly within the brain: glucosylceramide, a glucose-containing sphingolipid, was shown to bind and activate peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma in dopamine receptor D2-expressing medium spiny neurons of the dorsal striatum, and disruption of its synthesis caused depression-like behavior, whereas glucosylceramide administration reversed stress-induced depressive phenotypes (PubMed:41510157). In addition, polysaccharides from *Corydalis yanhusuo* alleviated chronic stress-induced depression-like behavior by reducing hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis overactivation, suppressing microglial activation, limiting harmful astrocyte transformation, and preserving hippocampal synaptic integrity, indicating that complex carbohydrates may modulate neuroimmune processes central to depression (PubMed:40513699). Although not a carbohydrate-binding study per se, the demonstration that hippocampal and neocortical deletion of astrocyte elevated gene-1 causes depressive behavior together with impaired dendritic structure and excitatory synaptic transmission is consistent with the broader view that pathways influencing extracellular recognition and neural morphology, including glycan-related interactions, may be relevant to depressive disease biology (PubMed:40122859). Overall, the available evidence suggests that carbohydrate binding may be related to depression because carbohydrate-recognizing proteins and carbohydrate-derived ligands participate in inflammatory sensing, barrier dysfunction, tryptophan metabolism, monoamine regulation, stress signaling, glial reactivity, and neuronal plasticity, all of which are established components of depressive pathogenesis.[PubMed:41500316](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41500316) [PubMed:33312105](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33312105) [PubMed:40101844](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40101844) [PubMed:41155365](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41155365) [PubMed:41794258](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41794258) [PubMed:41510157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41510157) [PubMed:40513699](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40513699) [PubMed:40122859](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40122859) 

Consistent with this broader literature context, there were 11 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the molecular function category of carbohydrate binding, a function defined by the selective and non-covalent recognition of carbohydrate structures ranging from simple sugars to complex oligosaccharides, polysaccharides, and chemically modified glycan derivatives. This enrichment is biologically notable because carbohydrate-dependent recognition operates at the interface of cell surfaces and the extracellular environment, where it influences several processes that are highly relevant to depression, including immune recognition, receptor activation, cell adhesion, intercellular communication, trafficking, synapse formation, glial responses, barrier signaling, and gut-brain communication. In the context of depression, the identification of 11 proteins in this functionally coherent category supports a mechanistic framework in which glycan-sensitive proteins may connect neuroinflammation, stress-related signaling disruption, synaptic dysfunction, and peripheral-to-central immune communication, thereby extending the interpretation of depression beyond neurotransmitter-centered models toward a broader systems-level pathology.

To further contextualize these 11 proteins, the figure below illustrates their protein-protein interaction network, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network inspection and functional exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/df893cca-0300-49b9-b8df-d347c044deb1.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=565C1ED811DA8975)

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified several significant proteins. We introduce them in detail below, moving from proteins with more direct immune-inflammatory relevance to those whose connections to depression may be more indirect or context-dependent.

CLEC4D is among the most compelling proteins in this list with respect to depression because it sits at the intersection of innate immune sensing, inflammatory signal amplification, and adaptive immune polarization. Binding of microbial ligands such as mycobacterial trehalose 6,6'-dimycolate and *Candida albicans* alpha-mannans activates FCER1G-dependent immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif signaling, leading to spleen associated tyrosine kinase, caspase recruitment domain family member 9, and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation and subsequent promotion of T helper 1 and T helper 17 oriented immune responses. This is highly relevant to depression because a substantial body of evidence links depressive symptomatology to chronic low-grade inflammation, exaggerated innate immune activation, and increased cytokine pathways that can alter monoamine metabolism, glutamatergic signaling, neuroendocrine function, and neuroplasticity. In particular, T helper 17 associated inflammation has been increasingly implicated in stress-related neuroinflammation and blood-brain barrier dysregulation. Therefore, CLEC4D appears to be a plausible upstream contributor to inflammatory states that may increase vulnerability to depression, especially in contexts involving infection, dysbiosis, or persistent immune activation. Its endocytic and antigen-presentation roles further support a broader function in sustaining immune responses that could influence depression-related immune phenotypes.[PubMed:23602766](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23602766) [PubMed:23911656](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23911656) [PubMed:14971047](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14971047) 

In contrast to CLEC4D, which may amplify inflammatory signaling, LGALS1 appears more consistent with an immunoregulatory role that could potentially counter excessive inflammation.

LGALS1 (galectin-1) is particularly relevant to depression because it is an immunoregulatory lectin with potent effects on T-cell fate and inflammatory balance. Its ability to induce T-cell apoptosis and suppress T helper 17 differentiation suggests a role in limiting excessive inflammatory responses. This is important in depression, where immune dysregulation is often characterized not only by elevated inflammatory mediators but also by altered T-cell profiles and disturbed immune homeostasis. By restraining T helper 17 associated pathways, LGALS1 may counter mechanisms linked to neuroinflammation, microglial activation, and cytokine-driven changes in neurotransmission. In addition, its broader roles in apoptosis and cellular differentiation suggest potential relevance to tissue remodeling and stress responses beyond the immune compartment. Thus, LGALS1 stands out as a candidate modulator that could influence depression risk or severity through anti-inflammatory and immunoregulatory mechanisms, especially in inflammatory subtypes of depression.[PubMed:24752896](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24752896) 

Shifting from immune regulation toward vascular and degenerative biology, COLEC12 may be relevant in a somewhat different but still biologically plausible manner.

COLEC12 is notable because it links innate immunity, vascular biology, and potentially neurodegenerative processes, all of which have plausible relevance to depression. Its role in recognizing pathogens and promoting phagocytosis places it within inflammatory host-defense pathways that can contribute to peripheral immune activation. More importantly, its capacity to internalize oxidatively modified low-density lipoprotein suggests involvement in oxidative stress and vascular inflammation, both of which are strongly associated with depression, particularly late-life depression and depression comorbid with cardiometabolic disease. The additional suggestion that COLEC12 may contribute to amyloid-beta clearance further increases its relevance, since depression is epidemiologically and mechanistically linked to cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease. Taken together, COLEC12 may be relevant to depression through inflammatory, vascular, and neurodegeneration-associated mechanisms rather than through a direct neurotransmitter-related pathway.

A related but distinct immune context is represented by SIGLEC1, which may be more informative for antiviral and interferon-associated inflammatory states.

SIGLEC1 is relevant to depression primarily because it reflects activated myeloid and dendritic-cell states associated with antiviral immune responses. Infection and sustained immune activation are recognized contributors to depressive symptoms, and interferon-related or virus-associated inflammatory programs are especially well known to induce behavioral changes resembling depression. By facilitating viral capture and entry into activated dendritic cells, SIGLEC1 may participate in immune processes that sustain antigen presentation and inflammatory signaling. Although the function listed here is not specific to the central nervous system, it is mechanistically compatible with the broader infection-inflammation-depression framework, in which peripheral antiviral responses alter cytokine production and thereby influence brain function, mood regulation, and sickness behavior. Accordingly, SIGLEC1 may be indirectly informative for depression biology, particularly in infection-associated or interferon-driven depressive states.

Moving further from direct immune sensing, AMBP may connect carbohydrate-binding enrichment to thromboinflammatory and vascular processes that have also been implicated in some forms of depression.

AMBP may have a meaningful, albeit more indirect, connection to depression through coagulation-inflammation crosstalk. Depression has been associated in some studies with platelet activation, endothelial dysfunction, and altered coagulation profiles, especially in individuals with cardiovascular comorbidity. By inhibiting factor ten a dependent prothrombin activation, AMBP may influence thromboinflammatory pathways that intersect with systemic inflammation and vascular risk. Its inhibition of mast cell proteases is also noteworthy, because mast cells can amplify neuroimmune and stress-related inflammatory responses and have been proposed to contribute to blood-brain barrier dysfunction and neuroinflammation. Therefore, while AMBP is not a classic depression gene, its protease-inhibitory functions could be relevant in inflammatory or vascular subtypes of depression.

The next protein, MRC1, is of interest for a different reason, as the annotation provided points toward chromatin and neuronal structural regulation rather than the more typical immune interpretation.

MRC1 is highly interesting from a neurobiological perspective because the function provided here points to a chromatin-remodeling factor involved in neural development, progenitor-state transitions, and dendritic growth. Processes of chromatin remodeling and activity-dependent transcription are central to synaptic plasticity, stress adaptation, and neuronal structural remodeling, all of which are strongly implicated in depression. Reduced dendritic complexity and impaired neuroplasticity are recurring findings in depressive disorders, particularly in corticolimbic regions. Therefore, a protein involved in neuron-specific chromatin remodeling and dendrite-associated gene regulation may be relevant to depression through mechanisms affecting neuronal maturation, connectivity, and long-term transcriptional responses to stress. This makes MRC1 a potentially important candidate for understanding how epigenetic and developmental programs intersect with vulnerability to mood disorders. However, the annotation provided appears atypical for the canonical mannose receptor gene symbol MRC1, so interpretive caution is warranted.

Finally, LGALS4 appears to have the most indirect connection in this set, with its potential relevance emerging mainly through barrier integrity and tissue organization.

LGALS4 has a less direct connection to depression than CLEC4D or LGALS1, but it may still be relevant through barrier and cell-adhesion biology. Adherens junction organization is important for epithelial integrity, and disturbances in gut barrier function have been increasingly linked to depression via the gut-immune-brain axis. If LGALS4 contributes to maintaining tissue architecture and barrier-associated interactions, altered function could theoretically influence inflammatory tone, microbial translocation, and downstream neuroimmune signaling. Nevertheless, based on the functional information provided, the evidence connecting LGALS4 to depression is more speculative and indirect than for proteins with explicit immune-regulatory or neurodevelopmental roles.

### Colon; goblet cells[≥Medium] (HPA:0130892) 

The pathway described as colon goblet cells refers to the differentiation, maintenance, and functional activity of specialized secretory epithelial cells in the colonic mucosa that synthesize and release mucins and other protective factors to form the intestinal mucus barrier. In the colon, goblet cells are central to the first line of host defense because they generate the mucus layer that spatially separates luminal microorganisms from the epithelial surface, limits penetration of microbial products, supports epithelial repair, and helps preserve immune and metabolic homeostasis. Adequate goblet cell abundance and secretion are therefore essential for barrier integrity, regulation of intestinal permeability, and control of mucosal inflammation. Experimental studies further indicate that goblet cell status is tightly linked to microbial ecology, short chain fatty acid production, tight junction expression, oxidative balance, and enteric neuroimmune signaling. Because the colon is a major interface of the microbiota gut brain axis, disruption of goblet cells may promote barrier failure, inflammatory cytokine production, altered tryptophan metabolism, and abnormal neurotransmitter signaling, all of which are biologically relevant to depressive pathology. Conversely, restoration of goblet cell number or mucus production has repeatedly been associated with improved colonic homeostasis and better behavioral outcomes in stress related and inflammation related models of depression. 

Against this biological background, the literature provided here suggests a fairly consistent connection between the colon goblet cell pathway and depression through impairment of the intestinal mucus barrier and subsequent dysregulation of the microbiota gut brain axis. Multiple depression related animal models indicate that stress associated or sleep deprivation associated depressive phenotypes are accompanied by a reduction in colonic goblet cells, implying weakened mucus protection and barrier injury. Chronic sleep deprivation in female mice induced anxiety and depressive like behaviors together with decreased goblet cells, epithelial abnormalities, glandular atrophy, microbial dysbiosis, and fecal metabolic disturbances related to oxidative stress and inflammation, thereby linking goblet cell loss to mood related pathology in the setting of barrier disruption (PubMed:39767560). Similarly, chronic unpredictable mild stress reduced goblet cells and crypt architecture in the colon, whereas behavioral improvement after hesperidin treatment occurred together with restoration of goblet cells, reduced inflammation, and microbiota remodeling, supporting a functional association between goblet cell preservation and antidepressant like effects (PubMed:39136837). In female mice exposed to chronic restraint stress, prebiotic administration restored the stress induced decrease in colon goblet cells in parallel with improvement of anxiety related behavior and normalization of gut and blood brain barrier markers, suggesting that goblet cell dependent mucosal resilience may contribute to stress vulnerability, particularly in females (PubMed:36650644). 

This pattern is further strengthened by intervention studies that more directly connect goblet cell recovery with improvement in depression related phenotypes. In treatment resistant depression models, synbiotic treatment with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii plus fructo oligosaccharides and galacto oligosaccharides increased mucus producing goblet cells while simultaneously reducing neuroinflammation, normalizing monoamine and gamma aminobutyric acid signaling, and reversing depression like behavior (PubMed:39214274). Likewise, short chain fatty acid supplementation rescued anxiety and depression like phenotypes induced by stress or fecal microbiota transfer and increased mucus producing goblet cells together with restoration of short chain fatty acid receptor signaling, reduced inflammatory cytokines, and correction of kynurenine pathway abnormalities, indicating that goblet cell recovery may be part of a broader therapeutic restoration of gut barrier and brain function (PubMed:38382546). Additional studies support this same general framework. Coprococcus eutactus treatment in adolescent stress exposed mice recovered goblet cells and mucus secretion while shifting tryptophan metabolism away from neurotoxic kynurenine products and improving depressive behavior (PubMed:38649105), and fecal microbiota transplantation in post stroke depression increased goblet cells while improving depressive like behavior and neuroinflammation (PubMed:40189067). Although some studies concern depression secondary to colitis or neurological disease rather than primary major depression, they still converge on a similar mechanism, showing that therapies which increase goblet cells also reduce colonic and cerebral inflammation, improve tight junction integrity, normalize hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis or brain derived neurotrophic factor related signaling, and alleviate depression like behavior (PubMed:40188913, PubMed:39647733, PubMed:41977455, PubMed:40145348). Taken together, these findings support the interpretation that colon goblet cells may be more than histological markers of intestinal health and could participate actively in depression relevant biology by maintaining the mucus barrier, restraining inflammation, shaping microbial metabolites, and stabilizing gut to brain communication.[PubMed:39767560](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39767560) [PubMed:39136837](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39136837) [PubMed:36650644](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36650644) [PubMed:39214274](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39214274) [PubMed:38382546](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38382546) [PubMed:38649105](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38649105) [PubMed:40189067](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40189067) [PubMed:40188913](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40188913) [PubMed:39647733](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39647733) [PubMed:41977455](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41977455) [PubMed:40145348](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40145348) 

Consistent with the literature based observations above, the enrichment analysis also points to a quantitatively substantial convergence on this pathway. There were 23 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway described as colon goblet cells, a biological program centered on the differentiation, maintenance, and secretory activity of specialized epithelial cells that sustain the colonic mucus barrier, regulate intestinal permeability, constrain mucosal inflammation, and influence microbiota gut brain axis signaling processes that are highly relevant to depressive pathology. Enrichment across 23 proteins suggests a meaningful concentration of depression associated molecular signals in intestinal barrier biology and supports the possibility that mucus layer integrity, microbial separation from the epithelium, cytokine control, oxidative balance, tryptophan metabolism, and neurotransmitter related signaling may collectively contribute to depression associated molecular dysfunction in this dataset. The figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 23 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for direct network inspection and functional exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/4eb2273b-7d08-4956-b027-6ca9e7e812ad.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=C556A7268DF93348)

With this network context in place, the following section introduces several of the significant proteins in greater detail and considers their possible relevance to depression in a cautious and evidence guided manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

YAP1 is particularly noteworthy in the context of depression because its reported activation of the ERBB4 C-terminal fragment links it to neuregulin and ERBB family signaling, a pathway with established relevance to synaptic plasticity, interneuron function, and higher order affective regulation. ERBB4 signaling has been repeatedly implicated in neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric processes, and perturbation of these pathways may influence cortical circuit stability and stress responsiveness. Although the functional statement provided here is concise, the YAP1 and ERBB4 connection appears biologically meaningful because depression is increasingly understood as a disorder of maladaptive neuroplasticity rather than solely monoamine imbalance. A protein that modulates ERBB4 activity may therefore contribute to altered neuronal signaling, resilience, and mood related circuit remodeling. For this reason, YAP1 stands out as one of the more directly neuropsychiatrically relevant proteins in the present list, even though no PubMed citation was supplied in the source annotation.  

A related but distinct line of reasoning points toward inflammatory and cellular stress pathways. LGALS3, galectin 3, is among the strongest candidates for relevance to depression because it integrates inflammation, cellular stress responses, and autophagy related membrane damage sensing. Contemporary models of depression emphasize the contribution of chronic low grade inflammation, altered innate immune signaling, and dysregulated neuroimmune crosstalk. A protein that promotes monocyte and macrophage chemoattraction, mast cell activation, and neutrophil associated inflammatory programs could plausibly contribute to systemic and central inflammatory states associated with depressive symptomatology. Its additional role in pre messenger ribonucleic acid splicing suggests a broader capacity to influence stress responsive gene expression, while its cooperation with TRIM16, ATG16L1, and BECN1 connects it to autophagic quality control pathways that are increasingly implicated in neuronal homeostasis and resilience under stress. Thus, LGALS3 appears important because it lies at the intersection of inflammation, intracellular damage responses, and transcriptional and post transcriptional regulation, all of which are mechanistically relevant to depression pathophysiology.  

Extending this theme, TSPAN8 may also be relevant because it converges on several biological systems now recognized as important in mood disorders, including inflammatory cytokine processing, mechanistic target of rapamycin and protein kinase B signaling, apoptosis and autophagy balance, and intestinal barrier integrity. Its role in promoting ADAM17 mediated tumor necrosis factor alpha processing is notable because tumor necrosis factor alpha is one of the most consistently studied inflammatory mediators in depression. In parallel, the interaction with RICTOR and mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 2 is significant because mechanistic target of rapamycin pathway dysfunction has been linked to impaired synaptic plasticity and to antidepressant mechanisms, particularly rapid acting antidepressant responses. The reported effect on apoptosis and autophagy further strengthens its relevance, as stress related neuronal vulnerability often involves maladaptive cell survival signaling. Finally, its role in intestinal epithelial barrier maintenance and regulation of intestinal inflammation raises the possibility of gut brain axis involvement, an area of growing interest in depression research. Collectively, TSPAN8 stands out as a multifunctional regulator connecting immune, metabolic, and signaling pathways with plausible mechanistic links to depressive illness.  

Shifting from inflammatory signaling to cellular energetics, CHCHD10 is of interest for depression because mitochondrial dysfunction is a recurrent theme in the biology of stress related and mood disorders. The maintenance of mitochondrial organization and cristae architecture is essential for oxidative phosphorylation, adenosine triphosphate production, calcium buffering, and apoptotic signaling. In neurons, which are highly energy dependent, even subtle disruption of mitochondrial ultrastructure can impair synaptic transmission and plasticity, thereby affecting neural circuits involved in mood regulation. Depression has been associated with altered bioenergetics, oxidative stress, and reduced cellular resilience. Therefore, a protein implicated in preserving mitochondrial integrity may be mechanistically relevant to disease susceptibility or progression. Although the annotation is brief and lacks direct citations, CHCHD10 stands out because mitochondrial homeostasis provides a compelling bridge between cellular stress biology and depressive phenotypes.  

In comparison with the proteins above, AGR3 appears to have a more indirect and tentative connection to depression. AGR3 is not a classic depression gene, but it may still be of interest because calcium regulation is a core biological process in excitability, secretion, and stress signaling. The function provided here is centered on airway epithelial physiology rather than neural tissue. However, the mention of intracellular calcium regulation is notable given the broader importance of calcium dynamics in neuronal communication and plasticity. In depression research, dysregulated calcium signaling has been linked to altered synaptic function and stress reactivity. Nevertheless, because the annotated role of AGR3 is primarily peripheral and respiratory, its connection to depression is likely weaker and more speculative than for proteins directly involved in inflammation, mitochondrial function, or canonical neuropsychiatric signaling pathways.  

Another protein with somewhat broader neurobiological relevance is BSG, which stands out because its functions map onto several processes potentially relevant to depression, including axon integrity, myelin maintenance, neuronal survival, and neurite remodeling. Disturbances in white matter organization, connectivity, and structural plasticity have been reported in depressive disorders, and proteins involved in preserving myelinated axons may therefore have pathophysiological significance. The anti apoptotic effect on neurons and the regulation of neurite outgrowth are also relevant, since depression has been linked to reduced neuroplasticity and stress induced neuronal atrophy. At the same time, the inhibitory effect on neurite extension suggests a complex role in shaping connectivity rather than simply promoting regeneration. Overall, BSG appears important because it participates in neuron glia interactions and structural maintenance of neural circuits, processes that may influence vulnerability to mood dysregulation.[PubMed:12089450](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12089450) [PubMed:27922006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27922006) [PubMed:7533044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7533044) [PubMed:10625334](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10625334) [PubMed:7516497](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7516497) [PubMed:9262180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9262180) [PubMed:9469574](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9469574) [PubMed:9482781](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482781) [PubMed:9482783](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482783) [PubMed:26335717](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26335717) [PubMed:15953602](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15953602) [PubMed:19158290](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19158290) [PubMed:17640868](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17640868)  

Moving from structural neural maintenance to vascular and trophic signaling, COL18A1 is potentially relevant to depression through vascular and neurotrophic mechanisms. Its anti angiogenic activity, particularly its inhibition of VEGFA signaling, is important because vascular endothelial growth factor has been implicated in neurogenesis, stress adaptation, and antidepressant responses. Although most annotations here concern endothelial biology, vascular endothelial growth factor related pathways are not confined to the vasculature and have recognized roles in the brain, including support of neurovascular coupling and hippocampal plasticity. Therefore, a factor that antagonizes VEGFA signaling could theoretically influence neurobiological resilience, tissue repair, or the neurovascular components of depressive pathology. This makes COL18A1 an interesting candidate, especially in frameworks that conceptualize depression as involving impaired plasticity and altered neurovascular support.[PubMed:9459295](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [PubMed:11257123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123)  

A somewhat related stress biology perspective is provided by RNASE1, which may be relevant to depression because it is explicitly involved in stress responsive intracellular regulation and redox homeostasis. Oxidative stress and impaired cellular stress adaptation are well established features in many patients with depression. The ability of this inhibitor to regulate angiogenin differently under basal versus stress conditions suggests a finely tuned mechanism linking stress exposure to ribonucleic acid metabolism, cytoprotection, and possibly translational control. Its putative role in redox homeostasis further strengthens the connection, as redox imbalance can impair neuronal function and plasticity. While the depression link is indirect, RNASE1 remains biologically compelling because it participates in molecular stress adaptation pathways that may shape vulnerability or resilience in mood disorders.[PubMed:12578357](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12578357) [PubMed:14515218](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14515218) [PubMed:3219362](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3219362) [PubMed:3243277](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3243277) [PubMed:3470787](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3470787) [PubMed:9050852](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9050852) [PubMed:17292889](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17292889) [PubMed:23843625](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23843625) [PubMed:32510170](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32510170)  

From there, the remaining proteins appear to have more contextual or peripheral links to depression. CXADR has a more speculative but still potentially meaningful connection to depression because infection and immune activation are increasingly recognized as contributors to depressive symptoms in a subset of patients. A host receptor that mediates viral entry may be relevant in the context of infection triggered inflammation, sickness behavior, or post infectious neuropsychiatric sequelae. However, based on the function provided, the link to depression is indirect and substantially weaker than that of proteins involved in inflammatory signaling, mitochondrial maintenance, or neuroplasticity. Thus, CXADR is best regarded as a peripheral or contextual candidate rather than a central mechanistic driver.  

Finally, PIGR may be relevant to depression through mucosal immunity and the gut brain axis, which returns conceptually to the barrier centered theme of this pathway. Secretory immunoglobulin A is a central component of barrier immunity at mucosal surfaces, and disturbances in mucosal immune regulation have been proposed to influence systemic inflammation and microbiome host interactions, both of which may affect mood and behavior. Although the function provided is immunological rather than neural, depression is increasingly viewed as a multisystem disorder in which peripheral immune and barrier processes can shape central nervous system outcomes. PIGR is therefore of moderate interest as a marker of mucosal immune homeostasis, though its mechanistic connection to depression is less direct than that of inflammatory signaling or neuronal plasticity regulators.
